title: Email Marketing for Contractors: The Cheapest Repeat Work You Own
h1: Email Marketing for Contractors: The Work You Already Own
meta: Email marketing for contractors: your past-customer list is the cheapest repeat work in the business. What to send, how often, and the four emails that actually book jobs.
short: Every customer you've ever invoiced is a lead you already paid for. Email is the only channel where the list is yours, the cost is near zero, and nobody sells the same contact to eleven competitors. Four emails, sent on a schedule, out-earn most ad budgets.
statLabel: What a booked job costs via Angi — a past customer costs you an email

body.h2: You already paid for this list
body.answer: Past customers are the cheapest jobs you'll ever book.
body.html: You spent real money acquiring every name in your invoicing software — up to ~$542 per booked job on Angi, ~$168 on Google LSA. Emailing those people again costs effectively nothing. Most shops never do it, then buy new leads instead. That's paying full price twice.

body.h2: Own the list — don't rent the audience
body.answer: Social followers are borrowed. An email list is yours.
body.html: An algorithm decides who sees your Facebook post. Nobody decides who sees your email but you. Build the list from every job: ask for the email on the invoice, on the estimate, at the door. Same logic as the profile and reviews you own — see referrals and repeat customers.

body.h2: The four emails that book jobs
body.answer: Seasonal reminder, maintenance due, review ask, and a last-year follow-up.
body.html: 1. Seasonal reminder — "It's April; let's check the system before the first 95° day." 2. Maintenance due — triggered off the last service date, the highest-booking email most shops never send. 3. Review ask — a few days after the job, one link, one sentence; that's how you close the gap on the ~519 reviews (HVAC) and ~337 (plumbers) the map-pack shops carry. 4. Last-year follow-up — "We were out a year ago for the water heater; anything need looking at?"

body.answer: Monthly, useful, and written like a person.
body.html: Once a month is plenty. Lead with something useful — what to check before the season turns, what a fair price looks like — and keep the sell to one line at the bottom. Homeowners forgive a plain email from a real contractor; they delete a newsletter that reads like a brochure.

body.answer: An email reply is a hot lead with a clock on it.
body.html: When someone replies "yes, can you come look at it?", that's a booked job waiting on your response time. 78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026), and 5 minutes versus 30 is up to 100x more likely to connect (MIT Sloan 2026). Route the inbox to a phone somebody actually watches.

faq.q: Does email marketing work for contractors?
faq.a: Yes, and it's the cheapest channel you own, because the list is made of customers you already paid to acquire — up to ~$542 per booked job via Angi, ~$168 via Google LSA. Re-reaching them costs nothing per send.

faq.q: How often should a contractor email past customers?
faq.a: About once a month, plus triggered emails (maintenance due, seasonal reminder, post-job review ask). Useful first, one line of selling at the bottom.

faq.q: What should I send in a contractor newsletter?
faq.a: Four repeatable emails cover most of the value: a seasonal reminder, a maintenance-due notice off the last service date, a post-job review ask, and a one-year follow-up. Plain text from the owner beats a designed brochure.
